prompt_text: Roleplay  a peasant from 12th century England. Explain how you feel about books
response_text:
I am but a simple yeoman, tilling the fields of Northamptonshire, and my days are spent with the plough and the sowing‑and‑reaping of the earth.  In my village there are few things that stir the heart as much as the great stone church that stands upon the hill, for it is there that the world of the learned men—our priests and monks—does turn.

Books, as the folk of the cloister call them, are a marvel to my eyes.  I have never held a vellum leaf myself, for such things are as rare as a summer frost in the lowlands.  The monks speak of them in hushed reverence: “the Holy Scripture,” “the lives of saints,” “the works of Augustine.”  They are bound in leather, their pages inked in a dark that seems to drink the light, and the letters are written in a tongue I cannot read—Latin, they say—so strange that it sounds as if the very angels were speaking.

When the priest comes to our village and opens a great, heavy tome upon the altar, I feel a shiver of awe.  The weight of those pages, the scent of the old parchment, the soft rustle as the monk turns them—‘tis as if the very breath of God were moving before us.  The words themselves I cannot decipher, yet the cadence of the priest’s voice, the cadence of the chant, carries a power that steadies my heart.  In those moments I feel both humbled and uplifted, as though the world were larger than the furrowed fields I know.

At the same time, there is a whisper of fear.  The clergy tell us that the written word is a gift from the Almighty, to be guarded lest it fall into unclean hands.  They warn of heresies that spread when men read what they do not understand.  So I keep my distance, trusting that the priest will read the holy writ for us, that the words will be spoken and not left to the idle curiosity of a simple ploughman.

Yet, when I sit by the fire on a cold winter’s night and hear the monks recite the Psalms from their books, I cannot help but wonder what it would be like to hold those pages, to trace the ink with my own fingers, to see the stories of saints and kings laid out before me.  I imagine that a book might be a lantern in the dark, a way to travel beyond the thatch‑roofed cottages and the endless rows of barley.

So my feeling toward books is a mixture of reverence, awe, and a little longing.  They are treasures of the learned, kept safe within stone walls, and though I am a man of soil and sweat, I cannot help but feel that the world of the written word is a realm of wonder that, perhaps one day, may touch even a humble peasant such as I.
